newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan business survey shows sentiment improving.
newsitem.headline: Japan business survey shows sentiment improving.

text.p: A closely watched survey released on Wednesday by Japan's central bank showed the mood among big manufacturers is improving, but the outlook was clouded and economists saw no immediate rise in the nation's record low interest rates.

The Bank of Japan's quarterly survey of business sentiment, called the "tankan", showed managers divided in March, with major manufacturers becoming optimistic but their non-manufacturing cousins more wary.
"The message of the tankan is...the external sector is doing very well but everything else is still doing very badly," said Richard Jerram, an economist at ING Barings.
Firms across the board were pessimistic in their outlook for June, when the next survey will be done, which analysts attributed to uncertainty created by tax increases this month.
The tankan's key index for large manufacturers rose to plus two in March from minus three in the previous survey in November.
It was the first positive figure since November 1991.
But while the manufacturers' figure rose to the high end of the range that economists had forecast, the index for large non-manufacturers fell sharply to minus six, compared with zero in November.
The indices represent the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those which expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.
For June, the manufacturing index fell three points to minus one while the non-manufacturers' index slipped one point to minus seven.

Economists said the tankan -- which is seen as an important indicator of monetary policy -- would do little to prompt a tightening of interest rates at present, with the non-manufacturing sector so weak.

"This is a sign that we are likely to see a stable (discount rate) for several months to come, probably for many months come," said Jane Berryman, a senior analyst at financial information firm Technical Data.

The central bank has kept rates at historically low levels since September 1995, when the official discount rate, at which it lends to commercial banks, was cut to 0.5 percent in a bid to kick the economy out of four and a half years of recession.
Economists said manufacturers were doing well on the back of a weaker yen, which makes exports cheaper for overseas customers.
But they said the retail and distribution sectors had been disappointed by weaker-than-expected consumer demand ahead of the rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent on Tuesday.
They said that while the economy was continuing to recover, the tax increases would keep casting a shadow over business.

"The consumption tax hike initiated yesterday is going to be a severe crimp on the Japanese economy's prospects for the next couple of quarters...we'll see the economy continuing to move forward but in fits and starts," said Technical Data's Berryman.
